---
title: Themes
description: One theme file colors the whole of Atlas.
icon: Palette
---

A theme in Atlas is a single file that colors the entire app: the chrome, the code editor, the terminal, diffs, and syntax highlighting. There is no separate editor theme to keep in sync, and no third setting for the terminal.

## Pick a theme

Press <Kbd>⌘,</Kbd> to open Settings, then choose **Appearance**.

Atlas ships 15 themes, among them Rosé Pine, the three Catppuccin flavours, Tokyo Night, Dracula, Monokai, One Dark, and Vesper. Each card shows a theme as two orbs, its light variant and its dark one, each lit by the theme's accent colour.

Atlas wears **two themes**: one while it is light and one while it is dark. Click a card to use that theme for both. Click one of its orbs to set just that half, so a light theme from one family can sit beside a dark theme from another. A ring and a sun or moon badge mark the halves you have chosen.

**Colour scheme**, above the themes, decides which of the two Atlas is wearing. **Light** and **Dark** pick one, and **System** follows your operating system's appearance, switching as it does. Each option is drawn as a small picture of Atlas in the theme it would give you.

## A theme has one variant or two

A theme file carries a dark variant, a light variant, or both. A card shows one orb for each variant the theme has.

When the variant you asked for is missing, Atlas uses the theme's other one. That is the defined behavior of the format, not a failure: picking Light with a dark-only theme applied is not an error state, it just leaves the colors where they were.

<Callout type="info">
  Thirteen of the 15 built-in themes ship both variants. Monokai and Vesper are dark-only, so their cards have a single orb, and making either your light theme still shows its dark variant.
</Callout>

## Install a theme of your own

Put a `.toml` theme file in `~/.config/atlas/themes/`. It appears in the grid next to the built-in themes.

If the theme you want is written for somewhere else, **Import theme**, beside the grid, converts a shadcn, Zed, or VS Code theme into one of these files. See [importing a theme](/docs/themes/importing).

Atlas watches that folder. Save an edit to the theme you already have applied and the app repaints, with no restart and no reinstall.

<Callout type="info">
  A file that fails to parse is skipped rather than taken as a failure of the whole catalog. The other themes, built-in ones included, keep working, and the picker names the file it could not read and why.
</Callout>

## Colors you leave out are derived

A theme file has three levels, and only the first is required:

- **Base tokens**: the shadcn/ui token set: colors, radius, spacing, shadows, and fonts. 42 are required; the three font stacks are optional.
- **Palette**: eight named hues (red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, blue, purple, pink). Optional.
- **Theme keys**: 73 Atlas roles such as `syntax.keyword`, `terminal.ansi.red`, and `element.hover`. Optional.

Each level contains the one before it. A file that stops at the first is finished, and every level you add takes back a surface Atlas was working out for you.

<Mermaid chart={`
flowchart LR
    subgraph K["plus theme keys: up to 73, exact control"]
        subgraph P["plus palette: 8 hues"]
            B["base tokens: 42, required"]
        end
    end
`} />

Every theme key Atlas needs but your file does not set is worked out from the palette, then from the base tokens, then from an Atlas default. Nothing is left at a previous theme's color, and nothing renders unstyled.

That means a file with nothing but the base tokens is a complete, working theme. Set a palette on top of it and the syntax, terminal, diff, and status colors follow your hues. Set individual theme keys only where you want a specific result.

A small number of colors are not on that list at all. A status badge's tinted fill is its status foreground at 12%, so Atlas works it out rather than asking, and a theme steers it through the foreground key instead. See [what a theme cannot set](/docs/themes/tokens#what-a-theme-cannot-set).

## What one theme covers

The active theme drives Atlas chrome, panels and tabs, the code editor and its syntax highlighting, the terminal, diff and review views, status colors and the agent chip, charts, graphs, and the scrollbars.

Two surfaces stay outside it:

- **PDF page content.** The viewer's chrome follows the theme, but the page itself renders as the document was authored.
- **The Browser tab.** It shows real web pages in a native webview, and those pages carry their own styling.

A theme may also name fonts, as shadcn themes do. Your own font settings come first: a theme's font applies only where you left the font on its default, and the picker then says **From theme**. See [Settings](/docs/product/settings#typography).

File and folder icons are their own track, chosen in Settings → Appearance → **File icons**. See [icon themes](/docs/themes/icon-themes).

## If you have written a theme before

Two things work differently from most editors.

Atlas has **one theme rather than two** for each appearance. Elsewhere you pick a UI theme and a separate editor color scheme, and a mismatch between them is yours to fix. In Atlas a single file covers both, so the editor and the window around it cannot drift apart.

Atlas **derives what you omit**. A theme that only names its base colors is finished, not half-finished. You add palette entries and theme keys to take control of a surface, not to stop it being wrong.
